I'm 65 years old. I've been farming these fields for 40 years. I only went to primary school, but I know this land better than any book or extension paper. My farm is 20.4 mu — not tiny, but not big either. Seven people live in my household, though some of the younger ones work in town now, so I can't always count on their hands. Money is tight. Every yuan I spend on inputs is a yuan I don't have for medicine, for repairs, or for when something breaks.

This year, like most years, my main business is the wheat-maize double crop on 18 mu. The other 2.4 mu I keep for millet. My wife likes millet porridge, and it's good to have something that goes straight to the family table. If the market turns bad, at least we won't go hungry.

For the winter wheat, I'll plant around October 10th, when the soil is still warm but the nights are cooling. I use an improved wheat variety — I've been saving my own seed for years, but I bought fresh seed two years ago to keep the vigor up. Before planting, I hire the rotary tiller to chop the maize stubble and turn the soil. Then I spread one 50kg bag of compound fertilizer per mu as my base — that's what I've always done. Come March, when the wheat starts jointing, I look at the color. If it's looking a bit yellow, I topdress with half a bag of urea, about 20 kilograms per mu. All told that's roughly 17 kilograms of nitrogen per mu, plus the phosphorus and potassium from the compound. I don't weigh it on a scale — I know by the bag and the scoop.

I'll irrigate the wheat three times: once before winter if the autumn stays dry, once at jointing in late March, and once at heading in early May. Pumping from the well costs electricity money, so I watch the sky and talk to my neighbors about whether they'll water. But I won't skip the jointing irrigation. That's the one that really matters. I'll spray herbicide once in early spring, and if I see leaf disease by May, I'll add a fungicide. Harvest comes in early June. The family handles most of the cutting and hauling, but I hire two days of extra labor for the rush — you can't let wheat sit in the field if rain comes.

Then the hard part: maize. The window between wheat harvest and maize planting is maybe five or six days, sometimes less. I plant around June 12th, right after the wheat comes off. I always buy fresh hybrid maize seed every year — I learned that lesson long ago. Saved maize seed is just throwing away yield. At planting, I put down one bag of compound fertilizer per mu, about 50 kilograms, and then at the big trumpet stage in July I topdress with another 15 or 20 kilograms of urea. That's about 16 kilograms of nitrogen per mu total. Maize gets two irrigations — one at jointing if July is dry, and one at tasseling. The summer rains usually help, but you can't count on them. I spray herbicide right after planting, and if the corn borer shows up, I hit it with insecticide. I hire a small tractor with a planter to get it in fast, and I might need one extra day of hired labor. If the weather is decent, I expect about 480 kilograms per mu.

The millet goes on that small 2.4 mu plot. I plant it in mid-May with saved local seed. I spread about 25 kilograms of compound fertilizer per mu — half a bag — and water it twice. One spray of herbicide to keep the weeds down. The family handles all the labor with hoes. No hired hands for that plot. Should get about 230 kilograms per mu, mostly for our own eating.

Total cash I'm laying out this year — seed, fertilizer, pesticide, pumping electricity, machine hire, and the little bit of hired help — comes to about 10,600 yuan. That's a lot for me. I thought about cutting back on the urea topdress to save money, but I'm 65. I can't afford a bad year. I'd rather put a little too much fertilizer and waste some money than put too little and lose a whole crop. At my age, borrowing money to get through winter is not something I want to do.
